text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Rail traffic disrupted north of Helsinki after seven empty tanker wagons derailed near Riihimaki on Sunday evening. No one hurt, but hundreds of travellers forced to take the bus.
- Growth of shopping centres in the last twenty years has led to closures of hundreds of neighbourhood food shops in the Helsinki area while the number of petrol stations and kiosks has doubled. @
- Almost half a million Finns, approximately the population of Helsinki have changed their places residence in the last year, statistics show.
KAUPPALEHTI
- Merita Pankkiiriliike brokerage sees no improvement in Finnish foresty industry net earnings next year -- says depressed pulp prices still a big question for the sector.
- Partek CEO Christoffer Taxell says slight upturn in building activity is not yet a stable trend, and that next year construction is likely to remain at this year's level. @
- Major owners saved construction group Polar by lightening its debt load and raising its equity to assets ratio to over 31 percent -- making it a strong firm overnight.
- Protos economist Petteri Hirvonen says markka may have been pegged to ERM at too strong a rate.
DEMARI

- Foreign Minister Tarja Halonen cautioned against creating arrangements within NATO which would hinder efforts to develop Partnership for Peace and the alliance. Halonen voiced doubts about the Baltic states' plans for closer ties to NATO. @
AAMULEHTI
- Building industry association plans quality classification system to weed out shady players.
- Fines fail to deter Russian smugglers from continuing black-market trade in alcohol at Helsinki's Hietalahti square.
- Finns living near Russian border zone would like to narrow the zone which is up to 3 kilometres wide.
- Analysts polled by the newspaper think Merita bank shares may be trading close to their upper limit. @
- Finnish race horses eat more than they earn. TURUN SANOMAT
- Standard of health care provided by municipalities uneven and a matter of chance, says one leading doctor.
